notes: Eminent-domain valuation case; the tourist camp on Mrs. Blair's homestead is only relevant to damages calculation, no bearing on lodging law or its regulation.
Search-warrant/liquor-possession appeal; the rented tourist-camp cabin is only the crime scene, no discussion of lodging arrangements or their regulation.
Robbery appeal; appellant merely slept at a tourist camp awaiting a signal, no legal issue touching lodging or its regulation.
Murder conspiracy appeal; no tourist camp or lodging facts appear in the opinion beyond retrieval noise; irrelevant.
Cotton-theft appeal; a planned overnight stay at a tourist camp is only an evidentiary detail on the conspiracy/accomplice issue, no bearing on lodging law.
Election-contest case; a voter's operation of a tourist camp is used only to assess her residency for voting purposes, not to address lodging law.

Breach-of-contract case over a month-to-month lease of a commercial warehouse building used by a grain company; not a dwelling/rooms letting or lodging/boarding matter despite month-to-month tenancy doctrine discussed.

Nuisance-abatement appeal over a gambling club ('Ringside Club'), not a hotel/boarding/rooming house; only interprets which houses the reputation-evidence statute reaches, no facts about compensated dwelling occupancy.
Robbery appeal; the tourist camp is merely where the proprietor was robbed while renting a cabin, appeal turns on jury-panel procedure, no lodging-law issue.
Venue/plea-of-privilege appeal in an assault suit; tourist camps are just the locations of the alleged assault, no lodging-law issue.
Child-desertion appeal; appellant's stay at an Oklahoma tourist camp is only evidence of his whereabouts, no lodging-law issue.
Trespass-to-try-title dispute over land underlying a tourist-cabin business; holding turns on lease-assignment priority against an unrecorded oral land sale, not on the character of guest lodging.
Rape appeal; a night spent by the prosecutrix at an Oklahoma tourist camp is newly-discovered-evidence fodder on her chastity, no lodging-law issue.
Suit against city for delayed road construction damaging a relocated tourist camp/filling station; dispute is about municipal contract/tort liability, not lodging regulation.

holding_summary: Residents of Henrietta sought mandamus to force the city council to reopen a hearing on a permit already issued to S. A. Donnell for a 'transit camp and filling station' in a residential district, arguing it was a fire hazard and would depreciate nearby property. The court held Donnell was a necessary party who had not been joined, and separately held that under the zoning ordinance the board of aldermen had discretion whether to call such a hearing, so mandamus would not lie absent a showing of abused discretion.

quotes.text: Plaintiffs allege that the transit camp' erected by Donnell will work injury and damage and incur fire hazard to plaintiffs and other citizens in the vicinity, and will decrease the value oí their property.

Certainly a mandamus could not be issued to force the board of aldermen to call a hearing where they were vested with a discretion in the first instance as to whether or not the hearing was advisable, unless allegations were made and supported by evidence, tending to show that the officer or officers against whom a mandamus is sought had been guilty of abuse of discretion.

notes: Marginal: the zoning ordinance frames a tourist/transit camp as a potential fire hazard/nuisance in a residential district (adverse-type regulatory posture), but the court reaches only procedural mandamus/necessary-party grounds and never characterizes the guest-occupancy arrangement itself, hence characterization left null.
Burglary appeal; appellant and a companion spending a night at a Mineral Wells tourist camp is only an accomplice-witness detail, no lodging-law issue.
Zoning-validity case, but the excluded use is a gasoline/oil filling station in an 'apartment district,' not lodging or boarding of paying occupants; no letting/lodging facts.

holding_summary: The city sued to enjoin Hattie Miller from operating two hotels, the Metropolitan Hotel and Grand Central Annex, on the ground that she knowingly permitted prostitutes to ply their trade there, a nuisance under the statutes governing hotels, boarding houses, and rooming houses (Arts. 4664-4667). The Court of Civil Appeals upheld admission of the hotels' general reputation as evidence of the nuisance but reversed because the judgment ordered the hotels closed outright for one year without including the statutory option letting the owner, tenant, or lessee keep them open by posting bond.

quotes.text: This suit as originally filed was brought by the city of Abilene and H. L. De Busk, a citizen of Taylor county, against Hattie Miller to enjoin the latter from operating two hotels in Abilene known as the “Metropolitan Hotel” and “Grand Central Annex.”

Has the defendant, Mrs. Hattie Miller, knowingly permitted prostitutes to remain in the two hotels in question and ply their trade therein? Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘No.’ ” To this question the jury answered, “Yes.”

The court is empowered to order the closing of such house for one year “unless the defendants in said suit or the owner, tenant or lessee of said property make bond payable to' the state at the county site of the county where such nuisance is alleged to exist, in the penal sum of not less than $1,-000.00 nor more than $5,000.00, with sufficient sureties to be approved by the judge trying the case, conditioned that the acts prohibited in this law shall not be done or permitted to be done in said house.”

notes: Squarely adverse: hotels regulated/enjoinable as nuisances under police power; characterization left null because the court never classifies the legal nature of any guest's occupancy, only the propriety of nuisance abatement against the operator.
